content.text:
TCP congestion control stops senders from overloading the network. Each sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd), which caps how many unacknowledged bytes can be in flight. The send rate is roughly min(cwnd, receiver window) per round-trip time (RTT). The network sends no explicit rate signal, so TCP infers congestion from packet loss, rising delay or ECN marks.

A connection begins in slow start. Cwnd starts small (often 10 segments) and grows by one segment per ACK, which doubles it every RTT. This exponential growth quickly finds how much capacity is available. When cwnd reaches the slow-start threshold (ssthresh), TCP switches to congestion avoidance and grows cwnd by about one segment per RTT. This is the additive increase.

When TCP detects loss, it backs off. Three duplicate ACKs usually mean one segment was lost while data is still flowing. Fast retransmit resends that segment, and fast recovery halves cwnd instead of starting over. This is the multiplicative decrease. A retransmission timeout means severe congestion: ssthresh drops to half of cwnd, cwnd falls to one segment, and slow start begins again. This AIMD pattern makes the classic sawtooth and lets competing flows settle toward a fair share.

Modern algorithms refine this. CUBIC, the Linux default, grows cwnd as a cubic function of the time since the last loss, so it recovers quickly on fast, long-delay paths. BBR does not treat loss as its main signal. It measures bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, then paces packets to keep queues short. ECN lets routers mark packets instead of dropping them, which gives earlier and gentler feedback.
